Rack Stitcher: methodology and capture guide

How a top-to-bottom video of a server rack becomes one straight, sharp image of the rack, and how to film so it comes out well.

One pipeline, one set of settings. The same ten stages run on every video; nothing is tuned per video. Of 41 settings listed below, 8 are calculated automatically from the video, 26 are fixed in the code, and 7 are options the calling app can change. Call it with stitch_rack("vdo3_60fps.MOV").

1. Block diagram

Blue: choose framesGreen: alignOrange: composePurple: geometryPink: cropYellow: quality check

2. The stages

1
Scan the video

Reads every frame once, scores its sharpness (mean gradient of the central region) and stores its timestamp. Nothing else is kept, so memory stays small. Timestamps come from the file, so variable-frame-rate phone video (vdo3 averages 47 fps) is timed correctly.

Why: A blurred frame carries no usable detail; knowing which frames are sharp is the basis of everything after.

2
Pick keyframes

Splits the video into about 36 equal time windows and keeps the sharpest frame of each. Only these frames are loaded for stitching.

Why: Sharp frames give sharp ports and labels; a few well-spaced frames overlap enough and keep the job fast.

3
Match features

Finds SIFT features (after contrast enhancement) in every keyframe and matches them between neighbouring keyframes with a strict ratio test.

Why: Matched points are the only evidence of how the camera moved between two frames.

4
Chain homographies

For each neighbouring pair estimates a homography on the dominant plane, the rack front, with a strict inlier threshold, then multiplies the pairs into a chain so every keyframe is expressed in one coordinate system (the middle keyframe is the reference). This also fixes the size of the single canvas. If some neighbours cannot be matched (for example plain wall) the longest aligned run is kept; if even that fails it retries with denser keyframes.

Why: The rack front is flat, so one homography per pair explains the camera motion; the strict threshold ignores cables sticking out of the plane.

5
Compose

Warps the frames onto one canvas and joins each new frame to the mosaic along a minimum-difference seam found by dynamic programming (8 px feather). Brightness of neighbours is matched first. If the canvas would exceed the memory budget the frames are shrunk.

Why: Every output pixel comes from one frame. Averaging overlaps would ghost the cables, which sit in front of the rack plane.

6
Rough crop

Finds the largest dark, neutral region (the cabinet) and crops to it with a 12% margin.

Why: Limits the next steps to the rack, so the wall and boxes do not influence the geometry.

7
Straighten verticals

Detects near-vertical edges (rails, cabinet sides), finds the point where they converge, and applies a homography that sends it to infinity. If the edges are already parallel (front-on capture) nothing is changed.

Why: Stitching leaves the rack slightly keystoned; straight rails are the cue for a rectilinear image.

8
Level horizontals

Measures the tilt of near-horizontal edges (shelves, device edges) and applies a shear (y shifted in proportion to x), repeating until the residual is under 0.3 degrees. The correction is always applied to the original image, so it is interpolated once.

Why: Step 7 only fixes verticals, which makes the axes not quite 90 degrees apart; the shear restores that.

9
Final crop

Along the equipment rows the share of dark pixels per column is high on the cabinet's two side panels and lower across the equipment, so the first solid dark band on each side of the centre marks the cabinet side. The open door is excluded. Vertically it runs from the cabinet top to just below the base. Empty corners are trimmed.

Why: Gives a rack-only image of consistent framing for any video.

10
Quality check and save

Computes how the video was captured (speed, overlap, blur, rack size, drift, rotation, brightness jumps, alignment strength) from data already at hand, raises coded warnings W01 to W19 with advice, and writes the PNG.

Why: Tells the user, in plain words, what to change in the next recording.

5. Code recheck

The module was reviewed again end to end before this report. What turned up and was fixed:

AreaProblem and fix
Frame timestampsSpeeds and durations were computed from frame counts, which is wrong for variable-frame-rate phone video (vdo3 averages 47 fps). Now read from the file's timestamps.
Alignment on textureless framesOne pair of plain wall or floor frames made the whole run fail. Now the longest aligned run is kept (W19 says what was left out); denser keyframes are tried first.
False keystone correctionOn a front-on, already-straight rack the vertical correction invented a keystone from noise. Now edges that are already parallel are left alone (a test checks both cases).
Unknown tilt looked like 'level'When too few edges were found, the tilt was reported as 0. It is now reported as unknown (None) with warning W15.
MemoryA very large canvas could exhaust RAM. Frames are now shrunk to fit a budget (default 40 megapixels, W17), and a diverged chain of homographies is caught as an error.
Blur measureComparing each frame with the whole video's median flagged plain wall frames as blurred. Each frame is now compared with its nearest neighbours in time.
Robustness of the callArguments are validated, a failing progress callback no longer stops the stitch, and parallel calls are tested to give identical output.
Tests: python tests/run_tests.py renders videos from a rack image with a known camera path and checks the output against the truth: the stitched mosaic correlates 0.987 with the true scene; a straight rack is left alone; an injected keystone is straightened (edge convergence -6.1 to +1.1 degrees); 13 capture faults, injected one at a time, each raise their warning; the good video raises none. 26 of 26 checks pass.
Not covered: W10, W13, W14, W15, W16 and W19 were seen firing in the tests and on real videos but are not each triggered in isolation. The thresholds come from four real videos and are not a statistically validated set.
The short version. Lower the phone straight down, slowly, with the rack facing the camera: 0.15 screen-heights per second or slower, 15 to 30 s in total, at 1080p or more, starting with the lid and some wall in view and ending with the base and floor in view. The two best videos here (vdo3 and vdo4) were the slowest; the weakest (vdo2) was the fastest.

3. Do and don't: the filming guide

DO
DON'T

Start and end of the recording

Pace

Do

  • Lower the phone straight down (bend the knees) and keep it upright, facing the rack. This is how vdo3 and vdo4 were filmed.
  • Go slowly: 0.15 screen-heights per second or slower, 15 to 30 s in total. The two best videos ran at 0.07 to 0.09 (19 and 26 s).
  • Film at 1080p or more, 30 fps or higher. Small port numbers need the pixels.
  • Start with the lid and some wall in view; end with the base and floor in view. Hold each end for about 2 s.
  • Keep the whole cabinet front in view, side panels included, from the first frame.
  • Stand centred in front of the rack, at a steady distance.
  • Light the rack (room lights on) and lock focus and exposure on the rack before you start.
  • Open the door fully or remove it; nothing in front of the equipment.
  • Record two takes and keep the one with the fewest warnings.

Don't

  • Don't rush. Under 6 s, or faster than 0.25 screen-heights per second, blurs the ports (vdo2: 0.36).
  • Don't start above the cabinet looking down at the lid top; those frames are wasted (vdo2).
  • Don't stop early. The base and a little floor must be in view (vdo1 stopped at the edge).
  • Don't walk toward the rack while filming. The size should change as little as possible (warning above x2).
  • Don't swing sideways or rotate the phone: keep drift under 0.4 frame widths and rotation under 25 degrees.
  • Don't use digital zoom, filters or heavy "cinematic" stabilisation.
  • Don't point at windows or bright lights, and don't let auto-exposure hunt (sudden brightness jumps raise W09).
  • Don't film in 720p if you want port numbers (W02).
  • Avoid flash and glare on the equipment fronts.

Numbers in this guide come from the four sample videos and the synthetic tests; they are recommendations, not guarantees. No camera distance in metres is recommended because it was not measured here; the guide uses what was measured: keep the whole cabinet front in view.

Checklist before you press record

  • ☐ Room lights on, door open
  • ☐ Phone set to 1080p or higher, 30 fps or more
  • ☐ Focus and exposure locked on the rack
  • ☐ Standing centred, whole cabinet in view
  • ☐ Start at lid height, wall above visible
  • ☐ Lower straight down, 15 to 30 s, no stops or jerks
  • ☐ Finish with base and floor in view
  • ☐ Two takes; keep the one with fewer warnings

4. What triggers a warning

Every run returns result.warnings (readable lines) and result.warning_codes. Each message states what was measured and what to do next time. The limits are in rack_stitcher.quality.Thresholds and can be changed with stitch_rack(..., thresholds=Thresholds(...)).

CodeNameTriggers whenWhat to doWhat is measuredHowVerified
W01Video Too Shortduration < 6 sTake 15 to 30 s.Video lengthTimestamp of the last frame, read from the file (so variable-frame-rate video is timed correctly).tested
W02Low Resolutionshorter side of the video < 900 pxFilm at 1080p or higher.Shorter side of the frame, in pixelsFrame size as stored in the video file.tested
W03Moving Too Fastmedian speed > 0.25 screen-heights/sAim for 0.15 or less (best videos: 0.07 to 0.09).Camera speed in screen-heights per secondHow far the frame centre moves between neighbouring keyframes (from the chained homographies), divided by the frame height and the time between them; the median is used.tested
W04Low Overlapvertical overlap of neighbouring keyframes < 35% at the weakest pairMove slower and steadier.Vertical overlap between neighbouring keyframesOne minus the largest vertical step between neighbouring keyframes, as a share of the frame height; the weakest pair counts.tested
W05Blurry Frames> 8% of frames below 60% of the sharpest nearby framesSlow down, steady the phone, add light.Share of blurred framesSharpness of each frame (mean Sobel gradient of its central region) compared with the 90th percentile of the frames within half a second either side; frames below 60% count as blurred.tested
W06Distance Changedrack size in frame changes by more than x2Keep a steadier distance.Change of rack size in the frameScale of each keyframe's homography at the frame centre; the largest divided by the smallest.tested
W07Sideways Driftsideways travel > 40% of the frame widthStand centred, move straight down.Sideways driftRange of the frame centre's horizontal position across the keyframes, in frame widths.tested
W08Phone Rolledapparent rotation range > 25 degKeep the phone upright.Rotation of the phoneRoll angle of each keyframe's homography; largest minus smallest.tested
W09Exposure Changed> 20% of neighbour pairs need more brightness correction than allowedLock exposure; avoid windows and bright lights.Brightness jumps between neighbouring framesMean colour of the overlap between the mosaic and the next frame gives a gain; the share of pairs whose gain falls outside 0.85 to 1.18 is counted.tested
W10Weak Alignmentfewer than 30 matched features between neighbouring keyframesSlower, more light, sharper frames.Strength of the alignment between two framesNumber of feature matches that agree with the homography (RANSAC inliers) for each neighbouring pair; the minimum.seen, not isolated
W11Rack Top Cutless than 1% of the stitched height above the cabinetStart higher: lid and some wall in view.Free space above the cabinetDistance from the top of the largest dark, neutral region (HSV value < 85, saturation < 100) to the top of the stitched image, as a share of its height.tested
W12Rack Bottom Cutless than 1% of the stitched height below the cabinetKeep filming until the base and floor are in view.Free space below the cabinetThe same dark region's distance to the bottom of the stitched image, as a share of its height.tested
W13Alignment Retriedalignment only worked with denser keyframesMovement too fast or jerky.Whether alignment needed denser keyframesThe first attempt with about 36 keyframes failed and the window was halved until it worked.seen, not isolated
W14No Vertical Referenceno reliable vertical edges foundKeep cabinet sides and rails visible and in focus.Vertical edges (rails, cabinet sides)Line segments found by the LSD detector that are near-vertical and on the rack; at least 3 must agree on one vanishing point covering 15% of the line length.seen, not isolated
W15Tilt Not Correctedhorizontal tilt cannot be measured or > 1 deg remainsKeep shelf and device edges visible.Tilt of horizontal edgesLength-weighted median angle of near-horizontal line segments after levelling; unknown if fewer than 8 are found.seen, not isolated
W16Cabinet Not Foundcabinet side panels not foundWhole cabinet front in view and well lit.Cabinet side panelsShare of dark pixels in each image column along the equipment rows; a solid band (75% or more) is needed on each side of the centre.seen, not isolated
W17Image Downscaledcanvas larger than the memory budgetRaise max_canvas_megapixels or lower the video resolution.Size of the stitched canvasWidth times height of the canvas computed from the aligned frames, compared with the memory budget (default 40 megapixels).tested
W18Soft Focusmedian sharpness < 30Tap to focus, clean the lens, add light.Overall sharpness of the videoMedian of the same per-frame sharpness value used for W05.tested
W19Part Of Video Ignoredstart or end of the video could not be aligned and was left outKeep the rack in view from start to end.Part of the video that could not be alignedNeighbouring keyframe pairs with fewer than 20 matches split the sequence; only the longest aligned run is used and the rest is reported.seen, not isolated
On the sample videos: vdo3 and vdo4 raise no warnings. vdo1 raises W02 (720p) and W12 (base at the edge). vdo2 raises W03 (too fast) and W10 (weak alignment). These match what was seen by eye. "Tested" means the warning is raised by a synthetic video with that single fault in tests/run_tests.py; "seen, not isolated" means it appeared on real or test videos but is not triggered on its own by a dedicated test.
